八音盒不是手持樂器，操作依類型而定：圓筒式靠轉動或上發條使凸點撥動音梳；紙帶式須: A music box is not a hand-held instrument, and how you operate it depends on the type. On a cylinder box you turn the cylinder or wind the spring so that the pins pluck the comb. A paper-roll box takes a punched paper roll: you turn the handle and the roll is drawn through to play the tune. A disc box takes a metal disc, and as the disc turns it drives a ratchet that strikes the teeth of the comb. A digital box can load MIDI (Musical Instrument Digital Interface) files or be arranged in an app, and an electrical signal then controls the wheel that plucks the comb. The first thing a beginner has to understand is the limits: the tune is usually fixed, you cannot rewrite it freely or control dynamics, the tempo is often slower than the original song, and the sound needs a resonating case to be loud enough.
八音盒屬體鳴樂器，靠帶凸點滾筒或圓盤撥動調律好的金屬音梳發聲，音色接近拇指琴、鋼: A music box is an idiophone: pins on a cylinder or a disc pluck a tuned metal comb. Its timbre is close to the mbira, the celesta or the glockenspiel; large disc boxes also have a bell-like voice. Compared with others in the same family, it plucks the comb automatically from a cylinder or disc and cannot control dynamics, so it has no real rise and fall in volume. The common ranges are 18 and 23 notes; 40, 50, 72 and 144-note models also exist. Paper-roll boxes have a larger comb, so their overall range is lower. The volume has to be amplified by a resonating case: a movement running on its own is easily drowned by room noise, neighbouring pins shorten the ring of each note, and the tune usually runs slower than the original.
八音盒為體鳴自動樂器，發聲分類編號112.1，常見於歐洲／瑞士。它曾以投幣式版本: The music box is an automatic idiophone, sounding classification number 112.1, common in Europe / Switzerland. It once appeared in public places in coin-operated versions, and it also played automatically in music bars and restaurants; museums still demonstrate it in daily rotation. In modern repertoire, Karlheinz Stockhausen wrote 《Tierkreis》 for twelve music boxes. Historical recordings are also there to listen to, including a disc music box, a mechanical music box playing 《Auld Lang Syne》, and a vinyl record of boxes from two historical makers.
八音盒發聲體主要為鋼製音梳，梳齒經調律；圓筒式以金屬音筒上的凸點撞針撥動梳齒，唱: The sounding body of a music box is mainly a steel comb, its teeth tuned. On a cylinder box, pins on the metal cylinder pluck the teeth; on a disc box, projections on the underside of the metal disc drive a ratchet that strikes the teeth; on a paper-roll box, a punched paper roll passes over the pins and plucks the teeth. Some more elaborate boxes also hold a small drum or bells. The source does not state what the body, the outer case and the resonating box are made of; all it records is that a music box is an automatic instrument housed in a box, classified as an idiophone (112.1), from Europe / Switzerland.
八音盒的機械發聲概念可追溯至九世紀巴格達班·馬薩兄弟的水力風琴，以及十三世紀法蘭: The idea of mechanical music in a box goes back to the hydraulic organ of the Banu Musa brothers in ninth-century Baghdad and to a thirteenth-century Flemish device in which a cylinder with pegs struck bells. The instrument grew out of the musical snuffbox in the eighteenth century, and its French name originally meant “bells of music”. In 1796 the Geneva clockmaker Antoine Favre-Salomon replaced the set of bells with a pre-tuned metal comb, which made the box smaller and the timbre more complex. Disc models appeared after 1885, disc record technology took hold in 1887, coin-operated boxes entered public places around 1900, and the trade declined from 1910 as the gramophone spread. The twentieth century brought small, cheap boxes, and the twenty-first century added digital control.

A music box is an automatically played idiophone, Hornbostel–Sachs number 112.1. Inside the case a rotating cylinder with pins, or a metal disc, plucks the tuned steel teeth of a comb in order, and it can play automatically or by hand, usually driven by a wound spring. It developed from the eighteenth-century musical snuffbox, and in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries it was expensive because of the fine workmanship, popular among the nobility; later it was combined with jewellery boxes, mantel clocks and cabinets, and there appeared home, coin-operated and public-place models used in music bars and restaurants.
